title: CBC Interpretation: Start With the Cell Line and Clinical Question
bottomLine: A CBC is not one result. Interpret hemoglobin/hematocrit, leukocytes/differential and platelets as separate cell-line problems, then integrate indices, trends and symptoms before choosing the next test or disposition.
recognize: Anemia, leukocytosis/leukopenia and thrombocytopenia have different differentials and safety implications.
A falling value can matter more than a single mildly abnormal result when bleeding, marrow suppression or sepsis is plausible.
differentiate: Hemoconcentration can raise hemoglobin without increasing red-cell mass; dilution can lower it without true loss.
Neutrophilia, lymphocytosis and eosinophilia are patterns, not standalone diagnoses.
assessment: Assess bleeding, infection, medications, nutrition, pregnancy, kidney/liver disease, malignancy/therapy and baseline trends.
workup: Use red-cell indices, reticulocytes, smear, iron/B12/folate, hemolysis studies or marrow/specialty testing only when they answer the identified cell-line problem.
management: Treat instability first, then the cause. Stable abnormalities require cause-directed follow-up rather than reflex transfusion, antibiotics or hematology referral for every deviation.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulants, marrow-suppressive drugs and therapies that alter counts before attributing the result to disease.
counselling: Explain which cell line is abnormal and why a trend or additional test is needed before naming the cause.
followUp: Close the loop on repeat counts and cause-directed testing; urgent abnormalities require same-day escalation.
examTrap: Treating 'abnormal CBC' as one diagnosis instead of identifying which cell line is driving the risk.
oneLinePearl: CBC reasoning starts with the cell line, then the trend, then the cause.

title: Comprehensive Metabolic Panel: Interpret the Pattern, Not the Printout
bottomLine: A broad chemistry panel combines electrolytes, renal markers, glucose and liver-related analytes that answer different questions. Identify the dangerous abnormality first, then determine whether the pattern reflects volume status, organ dysfunction, medication effect or a chronic baseline before ordering more tests.
recognize: Potassium, sodium, glucose, creatinine and bicarbonate can create immediate safety issues; mild isolated abnormalities often require context and confirmation.
A single creatinine or liver enzyme result does not define chronic kidney or liver disease.
differentiate: Volume depletion, medication effects and acute illness can shift several chemistry values together.
Transaminases indicate injury, not synthetic liver function; creatinine is an imperfect filtration surrogate.
assessment: Assess symptoms, hydration/perfusion, medications, renal/liver history, diabetes, GI losses, diet/supplements and baseline laboratory values.
workup: Repeat/confirm clinically important unexpected results and use focused urine, endocrine, acid-base or imaging studies only when the pattern justifies them.
management: Treat life-threatening electrolyte/glucose/acid-base disturbances immediately while investigating cause; stable chronic patterns need longitudinal disease management.
medicationSafety: ACE inhibitors/ARBs/MRAs, diuretics, NSAIDs, SGLT2 inhibitors and many other drugs can materially change chemistry values and risk.
counselling: Explain that the panel is a collection of clues, not a single pass/fail test.
followUp: Trend only the values that answer a defined clinical question and act on deterioration promptly.
examTrap: Ordering a second broad panel instead of addressing the one dangerous abnormality already visible.
oneLinePearl: On a chemistry panel, prioritize what can harm the patient now, then explain the pattern.

title: Lipid Panel Interpretation: Convert Numbers Into Cardiovascular Risk Decisions
bottomLine: Interpret lipids in the context of established ASCVD, diabetes, CKD, familial hypercholesterolemia risk and overall cardiovascular risk. The treatment decision is not simply 'LDL high = statin' or 'LDL normal = no risk'.
recognize: Established ASCVD and other high-risk conditions can indicate lipid-lowering therapy even when one lipid value is not dramatic.
Marked triglyceride elevation raises a different immediate concern than isolated LDL elevation.
differentiate: Primary prevention and secondary prevention use different thresholds/intensity logic.
Unexpected severe dyslipidemia should prompt review of secondary causes and familial disease.
assessment: Assess smoking, BP, diabetes, kidney disease, premature family history, prior vascular disease, pregnancy plans and medications.
workup: Use fasting testing selectively when triglycerides or a specific calculation/question requires it; investigate secondary causes when the pattern is severe or unexpected.
management: Use current Canadian cardiovascular-risk guidance to select treatment intensity and follow response/adherence after therapy changes.
medicationSafety: Review statin interactions, muscle/hepatic symptoms when clinically indicated and pregnancy-specific medication decisions.
counselling: Explain absolute cardiovascular risk and expected treatment benefit rather than focusing only on a target number.
followUp: Repeat lipids at a clinically useful interval after initiation/intensification and reassess adherence/tolerance.
examTrap: Treating the lipid panel without first identifying whether the patient is primary or secondary prevention.
oneLinePearl: A lipid panel refines cardiovascular risk; it does not replace risk stratification.

title: Thyroid Function Tests: Know When TSH Is Trustworthy
bottomLine: TSH is the preferred first-line test for most suspected primary thyroid disease, but central/pituitary disease, pregnancy, severe non-thyroidal illness and assay/medication interference can make TSH alone misleading. Interpret TSH with free T4 when the clinical context requires it.
recognize: High TSH with low free T4 supports primary hypothyroidism; suppressed TSH with elevated free hormone supports primary hyperthyroidism.
Low free T4 with an inappropriately normal/low TSH raises central hypothyroidism concern.
differentiate: Biotin and selected medications can distort assays; acute illness can create non-thyroidal patterns without true primary thyroid disease.
Free T3 is rarely the first test for uncomplicated suspected hypothyroidism.
assessment: Review symptoms, pregnancy, pituitary symptoms, amiodarone/lithium, supplements/biotin, thyroid medication timing/adherence and recent severe illness.
workup: Use TSH first when the pituitary axis is intact, adding free T4 and cause-directed antibodies/imaging only when indicated.
management: Treat confirmed disease and repeat testing after physiologically meaningful intervals rather than reacting to values before steady state.
medicationSafety: Levothyroxine absorption/interactions and antithyroid-drug toxicity can confound follow-up interpretation.
counselling: Explain why thyroid tests may need repeat/paired interpretation rather than one result deciding treatment.
followUp: Recheck according to treatment change, pregnancy and disease context; avoid unnecessary repeated panels.
examTrap: Using a normal TSH to exclude hypothyroidism in a patient with suspected pituitary disease and low free T4.
oneLinePearl: TSH leads in primary thyroid disease; free T4 rescues you when the pituitary context changes.

title: Liver Enzyme Pattern Recognition: Injury, Cholestasis, and Synthetic Risk
bottomLine: Classify liver chemistry as predominantly hepatocellular, cholestatic or mixed before choosing the differential. AST/ALT reflect injury, alkaline phosphatase supports cholestasis after source confirmation, and INR/albumin/bilirubin answer different questions about function and handling.
recognize: Predominant aminotransferase elevation suggests hepatocellular injury; predominant alkaline-phosphatase elevation suggests cholestatic/infiltrative disease.
Falling AST/ALT can be falsely reassuring in severe acute liver injury if INR, bilirubin, glucose or mental status worsen.
differentiate: ALP may be bone/placental rather than hepatic; albumin is affected by inflammation/nutrition/renal loss.
Bilirubin can rise in both hepatocellular and cholestatic disease and should be interpreted by fraction and pattern.
assessment: Assess jaundice, pruritus, pain, fever, encephalopathy, bleeding, alcohol, medications/supplements, pregnancy and infectious/metabolic risks.
workup: Use cause-directed viral/toxic/metabolic/autoimmune testing and ultrasound when the pattern warrants it rather than ordering every liver test for every mild abnormality.
management: Treat the cause and escalate suspected acute liver failure, cholangitis or rapidly progressive disease.
medicationSafety: Do not stop or restart essential potentially hepatotoxic medications solely from one small enzyme change without risk-benefit review and the full pattern.
counselling: Explain that liver enzymes show injury pattern, not a direct percentage of liver function.
followUp: Trend abnormalities that answer a clinical question and refer persistent/progressive unexplained disease appropriately.
examTrap: Calling aminotransferase elevation 'liver failure' without assessing synthetic function and clinical status.
oneLinePearl: Read liver tests by job: injury, bile flow and synthetic function are different axes.

title: Cardiac Biomarkers: Myocardial Injury Is Not Automatically Myocardial Infarction
bottomLine: High-sensitivity troponin identifies myocardial injury; myocardial infarction requires injury plus compatible ischemic evidence. Interpret serial change, timing, symptoms and ECG together, and use BNP/NT-proBNP as heart-failure probability/risk tools rather than stand-alone diagnoses.
recognize: Troponin can rise with ACS, myocarditis, tachyarrhythmia, PE, sepsis, renal disease and other myocardial stress.
BNP/NT-proBNP is influenced by age, renal function, obesity and atrial fibrillation.
differentiate: A normal early troponin does not automatically exclude early ACS; a chronically elevated troponin does not automatically equal acute MI.
CK-MB is generally lower value than modern troponin for routine ACS diagnosis.
assessment: Assess symptom timing, ECG, hemodynamics, renal function, heart-failure signs and alternate causes of myocardial injury.
workup: Use the validated local serial high-sensitivity troponin pathway and additional imaging/testing based on ischemic probability and alternate diagnoses.
management: Activate ACS/acute-care pathways when clinical/ECG/serial biomarker evidence supports ischemia; treat alternate causes of myocardial injury when they are more likely.
medicationSafety: Do not give antithrombotic therapy solely for a troponin elevation before considering bleeding risk and alternative diagnoses such as aortic syndrome.
redFlags: Rising troponin with ongoing ischemic symptoms
counselling: Explain why repeat testing may be required even when the first marker is normal or mildly elevated.
followUp: Close pending serial markers and ensure the cause of myocardial injury is documented and managed.
examTrap: Calling every elevated troponin an NSTEMI without ischemic evidence.
oneLinePearl: Troponin says injury; the clinical syndrome says why.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society acute coronary syndrome and heart failure guidance

title: Tumor Markers: Use Them for the Right Cancer Question
bottomLine: Most serum tumor markers are not population screening tests and are rarely diagnostic by themselves. Use a marker only when a validated cancer-specific question exists—such as treatment response, recurrence surveillance or selected diagnostic support—and interpret it with imaging, pathology and clinical context.
recognize: Markers can be elevated by benign disease and can remain normal despite cancer.
The useful marker and threshold depend on the cancer type, treatment state and clinical question.
differentiate: Screening an asymptomatic average-risk population is different from monitoring a known malignancy.
A rising marker can trigger evaluation but does not independently prove recurrence or progression.
assessment: Clarify whether the patient has a known cancer, symptoms, high-risk genetic syndrome or a defined specialty monitoring plan before ordering a marker.
workup: Use cancer-specific guideline pathways and confirm clinically important changes with appropriate imaging/pathology rather than serial marker testing alone.
management: Refer suspicious cancer presentations through the appropriate diagnostic pathway; do not reassure or treat solely on marker status.
medicationSafety: Avoid invasive procedures or therapy changes based only on a nonspecific marker without confirmatory evaluation.
redFlags: Cancer alarm symptoms with a 'normal' marker
Rapid unexplained marker rise in known cancer
New organ dysfunction suggesting metastatic disease
counselling: Explain that tumor markers are imperfect and are usually used as one part of cancer monitoring, not as a universal cancer blood test.
followUp: Track any abnormal marker within the cancer-specific diagnostic or surveillance plan and document who owns follow-up.
examTrap: Ordering a broad panel of tumor markers to screen an asymptomatic patient for hidden cancer.
oneLinePearl: A tumor marker needs a validated cancer question before it needs a blood draw.
sourceBasis: Canadian cancer-specific diagnostic and surveillance practice

title: Inflammatory Markers: Move Probability, Do Not Name the Disease
bottomLine: CRP and ESR are nonspecific. Use them when a defined clinical question exists and when the result can change probability, urgency or follow-up; do not use an elevated value as proof of bacterial infection, autoimmune disease or occult cancer.
recognize: CRP changes more rapidly and is generally preferable for acute systemic inflammation; ESR is slower and more confounded by age, anemia, pregnancy and proteins.
Discordant markers can occur and should be interpreted through the disease context rather than normalized by ordering more nonspecific tests.
differentiate: Normal markers do not safely exclude time-critical disease when the clinical syndrome is compelling.
Selected diseases such as giant-cell arteritis use inflammatory markers as supporting evidence, not as the sole diagnostic criterion.
assessment: Define the suspected syndrome, pretest probability and the management decision that a high/low result would change.
workup: Use disease-specific tests, cultures/imaging or specialist evaluation when indicated rather than repeated CRP/ESR without a diagnostic hypothesis.
management: Treat the clinical diagnosis and patient severity; trend markers only when the trajectory has a validated role in management.
medicationSafety: Do not start/broaden antibiotics or immunosuppression solely because a nonspecific inflammatory marker is elevated.
redFlags: Clinical sepsis/organ dysfunction despite low marker
Visual symptoms with possible giant-cell arteritis
Persistent systemic illness/weight loss requiring definitive evaluation
counselling: Explain that inflammatory markers indicate inflammation but usually cannot tell the exact cause.
followUp: Stop trending when the result no longer changes care and reassess diagnosis when marker and clinical course diverge.
examTrap: Diagnosing bacterial infection from an elevated CRP without a compatible syndrome.
oneLinePearl: Inflammatory markers adjust probability; they do not finish the differential.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Medical Biochemistry recommendations

title: Coagulation Studies: Match the Test to the Drug and the Bleeding Question
bottomLine: PT/INR, aPTT, thrombin time, fibrinogen and platelet count answer different hemostasis questions. INR is designed for vitamin-K antagonist management, aPTT may guide UFH under a validated local assay, and routine PT/INR/aPTT cannot be interpreted as quantitative DOAC levels.
recognize: Bleeding can occur with normal routine coagulation tests and abnormal results can occur without active bleeding.
Drug exposure, liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency and factor disorders create different patterns.
differentiate: Platelet number/function and coagulation-factor abnormalities are different hemostasis problems.
A normal PT/aPTT does not reliably exclude clinically important factor-Xa inhibitor effect; thrombin time is very sensitive to dabigatran exposure.
assessment: Assess bleeding site/severity, last anticoagulant dose, renal/liver function, medications, pregnancy, prior results and procedural context.
workup: Order only tests that answer the bleeding/anticoagulant question; use validated drug-specific assays when available and when the result would change management.
management: Treat major bleeding and hemodynamic instability first while clarifying the anticoagulant/coagulopathy; use current reversal/transfusion protocols.
medicationSafety: Do not dose DOACs to INR/aPTT and do not assume a normal routine test means no drug effect.
Warfarin and heparin monitoring require the appropriate validated assay and indication-specific target.
redFlags: Urgent procedure with uncertain anticoagulant effect
counselling: Explain why different anticoagulants require different monitoring and why one 'clotting test' does not cover every drug.
followUp: Close the loop on reversal, renal clearance, repeat testing and anticoagulation restart decisions.
examTrap: Using a normal INR to prove a patient taking apixaban has no anticoagulant effect.
oneLinePearl: Coagulation tests are drug- and pathway-specific; there is no universal clotting number.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada — DOACs: Coagulation Tests and Management of Bleeding

title: Urinalysis: Interpret the Syndrome Before Treating the Dipstick
bottomLine: Urinalysis is an adjunct to a urinary or renal syndrome. Pyuria/bacteriuria without urinary symptoms often represents asymptomatic bacteriuria, while protein, blood and casts may signal kidney disease that should not be mislabeled UTI.
recognize: Leukocyte esterase/nitrite can support UTI when symptoms fit, but neither alone diagnoses infection.
Proteinuria, hematuria and casts require a renal differential, especially when persistent or accompanied by impaired kidney function.
differentiate: Cloudy/malodorous urine and bacteriuria alone are not sufficient reasons to treat most nonpregnant adults.
Dipstick blood may reflect red cells, hemoglobin or myoglobin and needs microscopy/context.
assessment: Ask dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic/flank pain, fever, pregnancy, instrumentation, stones, menstruation/exercise and renal/systemic symptoms.
workup: Culture symptomatic/high-risk patients when the result changes therapy; avoid routine urine culture in asymptomatic adults except defined pregnancy/urologic-procedure contexts.
Quantify persistent proteinuria and evaluate persistent hematuria according to renal/urologic pathways.
management: Treat the clinical syndrome, not the test strip; avoid antibiotics for asymptomatic bacteriuria outside accepted exceptions.
medicationSafety: Unnecessary antibiotics cause resistance, adverse effects and C. difficile risk.
NSAIDs/anticoagulants and other drugs can contribute to renal/hematuria findings and should be reviewed.
counselling: Explain why a positive urine test does not always mean infection and why symptoms matter.
followUp: Ensure cultures and persistent renal/urologic abnormalities are reviewed to resolution.
examTrap: Treating an older adult's positive urine culture for confusion alone without localizing urinary symptoms or systemic infection evidence.
oneLinePearl: Urine tests support a syndrome; they do not create one.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Medical Microbiology and Family Medicine recommendations

title: ABG Interpretation: Identify the Primary Disorder and Test Compensation
bottomLine: ABG interpretation is a physiology sequence: assess pH, identify the respiratory/metabolic driver, test whether compensation is appropriate, then integrate oxygenation and the clinical cause. An 'almost normal' pH can hide a dangerous mixed disorder.
recognize: PaCO2 moves pH in the acid direction; bicarbonate moves pH in the base direction.
Unexpected compensation suggests a second acid-base process.
differentiate: ABG defines acid-base/gas exchange but does not identify the underlying diagnosis by itself.
Venous blood gas can answer many pH/CO2 questions, while arterial sampling is needed when accurate oxygenation assessment matters.
assessment: Assess respiratory effort, oxygen delivery/ventilation support, hemodynamics, GI losses, renal disease, toxins, sepsis and medications.
workup: Use electrolytes/anion gap, lactate, ketones, toxicology and imaging according to the suspected cause.
management: Treat the cause and stabilize oxygenation/ventilation/perfusion; do not chase pH with bicarbonate or ventilator changes without understanding physiology.
medicationSafety: Sedatives/opioids can cause respiratory acidosis; diuretics/vomiting can contribute to metabolic alkalosis; salicylates can produce mixed patterns.
redFlags: Rapidly rising CO2 with altered mental status
counselling: When appropriate, explain that blood-gas values reflect how lungs and metabolism are handling acid/base and gas exchange.
followUp: Repeat gas testing only when trajectory or intervention response will change management.
examTrap: Calling a near-normal pH reassuring without checking whether PaCO2 and bicarbonate are both markedly abnormal.
oneLinePearl: ABG: pH, primary process, expected compensation, oxygenation, cause.

title: ECG Fundamentals: Rate, Rhythm, Intervals, Axis, Ischemia, Then the Patient
bottomLine: Use a repeatable ECG sequence and connect every tracing to symptoms/hemodynamics. Identify immediately dangerous ischemia, ventricular arrhythmia, high-grade block, severe electrolyte patterns and pre-excitation/QT risk before refining lower-risk abnormalities.
recognize: Systematic interpretation reduces missed rate/rhythm/interval/ischemia findings.
A machine interpretation is an aid, not the final diagnosis.
differentiate: ST elevation has ischemic and nonischemic causes; a normal ECG does not exclude early ACS.
Wide-complex tachycardia should be treated as ventricular until appropriately clarified in an unstable patient.
assessment: Assess chest pain, syncope, palpitations, dyspnea, medications/electrolytes, prior ECG and hemodynamic stability.
workup: Repeat ECG and serial troponin when ACS remains plausible; obtain electrolytes/other testing when conduction/QT/arrhythmia context warrants.
management: Treat unstable rhythms/ischemia through acute-care algorithms and use specialty follow-up for persistent conduction/structural concerns.
medicationSafety: Review QT-prolonging and AV-node-blocking drugs when the corresponding ECG abnormality appears.
counselling: Explain when an incidental ECG finding needs follow-up versus emergency assessment.
followUp: Compare prior tracings and ensure arrhythmia/structural disease workup is completed.
examTrap: Accepting the automated ECG label without checking the rhythm and clinical context.
oneLinePearl: Read the ECG systematically, then decide what the tracing means for this patient now.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society rhythm/ACS practice principles

title: Chest X-Ray: Quality First, Then a Structured Cardiopulmonary Read
bottomLine: Before interpreting a chest X-ray, check projection, rotation, inspiration and exposure. Then use a structured read for airway, lungs/pleura, heart/mediastinum, diaphragm and bones/soft tissues; a normal film does not exclude early pneumonia, PE or ACS.
recognize: Projection and poor inspiration can falsely enlarge the heart or create apparent basal opacity.
Pneumothorax, lobar consolidation, pulmonary edema and large effusions have pattern-based radiographic clues.
differentiate: Chest X-ray is not a rule-out test for PE or ACS and may be normal in early infection.
Portable AP films create different magnification/quality issues than standard PA/lateral imaging.
assessment: Interpret the image against symptoms, oxygenation, examination and prior imaging.
workup: Use CT, ultrasound or repeat imaging only when the clinical differential requires greater sensitivity/specificity.
management: Act urgently on pneumothorax, major edema, large symptomatic effusion or other acute findings; do not delay care waiting for a perfect radiology description in an unstable patient.
medicationSafety: Avoid antibiotics solely because of a nonspecific opacity without a compatible infectious syndrome.
redFlags: Rapidly progressive bilateral opacities with hypoxemia
Mediastinal widening with acute aortic concern
counselling: Explain that imaging findings are interpreted with symptoms and may require follow-up imaging for unresolved abnormalities.
followUp: Track radiology recommendations and unresolved opacities/nodules to completion.
examTrap: Calling a normal chest X-ray proof that PE, early pneumonia or ACS is absent.
oneLinePearl: Chest X-ray starts with image quality and ends with clinical correlation.
sourceBasis: Canadian radiology and respiratory practice principles

title: Abdominal Imaging: Choose the Modality That Answers the Dangerous Differential
bottomLine: Abdominal imaging is selected from the suspected diagnosis, patient stability, pregnancy/age, radiation/contrast risk and local access. Ultrasound is first-line for many biliary/pelvic/pregnancy/pediatric questions; CT is powerful for acute intra-abdominal pathology but should not replace focused clinical reasoning.
recognize: RUQ/biliary and many pelvic/pregnancy questions are well suited to ultrasound.
CT is often the key cross-sectional test for obstruction, perforation, complicated diverticulitis, ischemia or broad undifferentiated acute abdomen in appropriate patients.
differentiate: A symptomatic patient needs diagnostic imaging, not an average-risk screening pathway.
Radiation and contrast risk alter modality choice but do not justify delaying time-critical imaging when benefit is high.
assessment: Define pain location/onset, peritonitis, hemodynamics, pregnancy possibility, renal function/contrast history, prior surgery and the leading dangerous diagnoses.
workup: Choose ultrasound, CT, MRI or targeted plain radiography only when each can answer the clinical question; in children with suspected appendicitis, consider ultrasound before CT when appropriate.
management: Escalate surgical/obstetric/vascular emergencies while imaging is being arranged; imaging should support, not postpone, stabilization.
medicationSafety: Contrast and sedation decisions are individualized; avoid outdated blanket contraindications and review current radiology policy.
redFlags: Pain out of proportion/mesenteric ischemia concern
counselling: Explain why the chosen modality is best for the suspected problem and discuss radiation/contrast when relevant.
followUp: Track incidental or indeterminate findings and ensure urgent results reach the responsible clinician.
examTrap: Ordering the same abdominal CT for every pain presentation without considering pregnancy, biliary/pelvic ultrasound or the actual differential.
oneLinePearl: Pick abdominal imaging by the diagnosis you must confirm or exclude—not by habit.

title: Musculoskeletal Imaging: Image When the Result Changes Management
bottomLine: Most uncomplicated mechanical musculoskeletal pain does not require immediate imaging. Use red flags, trauma rules, persistent/progressive neurologic deficit and a specific treatment question to decide when X-ray, ultrasound, CT or MRI adds value.
recognize: Plain radiography is useful for many fracture/arthritis/bony alignment questions; ultrasound can evaluate selected tendon/effusion questions; MRI is useful for soft tissue, marrow, cord and selected persistent symptoms.
Degenerative imaging abnormalities are common in asymptomatic adults and may not explain pain.
differentiate: Uncomplicated low-back pain without red flags is not an automatic MRI indication.
Progressive neurologic deficit, cauda equina, infection, cancer or significant trauma changes the imaging threshold immediately.
assessment: Assess trauma, neurologic function, fever/infection risk, cancer history, osteoporosis/steroid risk, function, duration and whether imaging would change treatment.
workup: Apply validated trauma rules/pathways and reserve advanced imaging for a defined diagnostic or procedural decision.
management: Treat uncomplicated mechanical pain with activity/rehabilitation strategies while monitoring; escalate red flags to urgent imaging/specialty care.
medicationSafety: Avoid sedating analgesic escalation simply because imaging is deferred; imaging restraint is not undertreatment.
counselling: Explain that early imaging often finds common age-related abnormalities that do not improve recovery or identify the pain generator.
followUp: Reassess if symptoms fail expected recovery or new red flags emerge.
examTrap: Ordering MRI for two weeks of uncomplicated low-back pain with a normal neurologic exam.
oneLinePearl: Image MSK pain when a red flag or treatment decision needs an answer.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada low-back/spine imaging recommendations

title: Neuroimaging: Match CT or MRI to the Neurologic Emergency
bottomLine: Neuroimaging is chosen from onset, trauma, focal findings, vascular/infectious/cancer risk and the question being asked. CT is fast for hemorrhage/trauma and many emergencies; MRI is more sensitive for many parenchymal/posterior-fossa/demyelinating processes but should not delay time-critical stroke or hemorrhage care.
recognize: New focal deficit, thunderclap headache, head trauma, reduced consciousness, cancer/immunocompromise and signs of raised ICP change the imaging threshold.
Simple syncope with a normal neurologic exam and uncomplicated recurrent headache without red flags generally do not need routine neuroimaging.
differentiate: A normal noncontrast CT does not exclude all ischemic stroke, posterior fossa disease or other neurologic pathology.
Carotid imaging, brain CT and brain MRI answer different questions and should not be ordered as a reflex bundle.
assessment: Establish onset/last-known-well, trauma, focal exam, anticoagulation, headache pattern, seizure, fever, cancer/immune status and pregnancy where relevant.
workup: Use stroke/trauma/headache/seizure-specific imaging pathways and choose vascular imaging when vessel pathology is the question.
management: Do not delay emergency stroke activation or stabilization for nonessential imaging; act on hemorrhage, mass effect and vascular emergencies urgently.
medicationSafety: Contrast/sedation decisions are patient- and modality-specific; use current radiology policy rather than outdated universal exclusions.
counselling: Explain why imaging may be unnecessary for low-risk headache/syncope and when new neurologic symptoms change that decision.
followUp: Track incidental/indeterminate findings and ensure urgent imaging results have explicit ownership.
examTrap: Ordering CT head for every simple syncope or stable migraine—or waiting for MRI before activating an acute stroke pathway.
oneLinePearl: Neuroimaging is question-specific: choose the modality that changes the emergency or differential.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Radiology/Internal Medicine/Emergency Medicine recommendations

title: Ultrasound in Primary Care: Use the Modality for the Question It Answers Best
bottomLine: Ultrasound is valuable when it can answer a focused question without ionizing radiation—biliary, pelvic/pregnancy, effusion, bladder, DVT and selected soft-tissue questions—but a limited or negative study must not overrule a dangerous clinical syndrome when sensitivity is insufficient.
recognize: Ultrasound is operator- and body-habitus dependent and answers some questions far better than others.
Point-of-care ultrasound supplements the clinical assessment; it does not replace formal imaging or specialist interpretation when the question exceeds the operator's validated scope.
differentiate: A negative bedside scan does not safely exclude every PE, appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy or vascular emergency.
Formal diagnostic ultrasound and focused POCUS have different documentation, quality and credentialing expectations.
assessment: Define the clinical question, urgency, pregnancy/radiation considerations and whether a positive/negative result will actually change management.
workup: Escalate to formal ultrasound, CT/MRI or specialty evaluation when the bedside study is indeterminate or the clinical risk remains high.
management: Use findings within validated scope and local policy; stabilize emergencies rather than delaying for an optional scan.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary sedation/contrast by choosing ultrasound when it can answer the question, but do not avoid necessary definitive imaging solely to eliminate radiation.
redFlags: Persistent high-risk DVT/ectopic concern despite nondiagnostic scan
Operator uncertainty in an unstable patient
counselling: Explain what the ultrasound can and cannot determine and why another test may still be needed.
followUp: Document limitations and ensure formal follow-up for indeterminate or incidental findings.
examTrap: Using a limited POCUS result as definitive exclusion of a high-risk diagnosis outside the test's validated performance.
oneLinePearl: Ultrasound is strongest when the question is focused and the operator knows the limits.

title: CT: Use Speed and Detail When the Benefit Justifies Radiation and Contrast
bottomLine: CT is fast and highly useful for many emergency thoracic, abdominal, neurologic and traumatic questions, but it should be selected for a specific diagnosis that changes care. Radiation, pregnancy, renal/contrast issues and prior imaging matter, yet outdated blanket 'contraindications' should not delay life-saving imaging.
recognize: Noncontrast, contrast-enhanced, angiographic and low-dose CT protocols answer different questions.
Children and pregnancy require extra attention to radiation alternatives, but urgency and diagnostic benefit still govern.
differentiate: CT is not automatically superior to ultrasound or MRI; modality choice depends on anatomy, urgency and the suspected disease.
Contrast risk is individualized; prior mild reaction or CKD does not automatically prohibit all contrast-enhanced CT.
assessment: Define indication, pregnancy possibility, renal function when contrast decisions require it, prior contrast reaction and whether previous imaging already answers the question.
workup: Choose the correct protocol and avoid repeat CT when recent adequate imaging exists unless the clinical question changed.
management: Proceed urgently when benefit outweighs risk; use alternative imaging when it provides equivalent information with less harm.
medicationSafety: Contrast premedication and medication holds are protocol/patient specific; use current radiology guidance rather than universal rules.
redFlags: High-risk PE when CT angiography is appropriate
counselling: Explain why CT is being used, including radiation/contrast tradeoffs when time allows.
followUp: Track incidental findings and radiology recommendations to completion.
examTrap: Avoiding an urgently indicated CT because of a generalized fear of contrast/radiation without weighing immediate diagnostic benefit.
oneLinePearl: CT is a question-specific tool; protocol and urgency matter as much as the scanner.

title: MRI: High Soft-Tissue Detail, Strong Safety Screening, and the Right Urgency
bottomLine: MRI offers excellent neurologic, spinal, soft-tissue and many organ-specific assessments without ionizing radiation, but it is slower, less available and requires device/metal/claustrophobia safety screening. Do not delay a time-critical CT-based emergency pathway simply because MRI is more sensitive for another question.
recognize: MRI is particularly useful for brain/spinal cord, demyelination, soft tissue, marrow and selected abdominal/pelvic questions.
Implanted devices are not automatically unsafe; MRI-conditional status and protocol determine eligibility.
differentiate: MRI is not the initial test for every acute head/trauma/bleeding presentation.
Gadolinium contrast and MRI device safety are different issues and require separate assessment.
assessment: Screen implanted devices/metal, prior surgery/foreign bodies, claustrophobia, ability to lie still, pregnancy and renal function when gadolinium is planned.
workup: Choose MRI sequence/contrast according to the clinical question and use urgent alternative imaging when MRI delay would harm.
management: Coordinate device verification/sedation when needed and act urgently on cord compression, abscess, cauda equina or other critical findings.
medicationSafety: Sedation risk and gadolinium decisions are individualized; avoid routine sedation when communication/support can achieve the scan safely.
redFlags: Device status unknown with urgent MRI request
Unstable patient who cannot safely tolerate scanner delay
counselling: Explain the magnetic-field/device questions and why another modality may be safer/faster in some emergencies.
followUp: Track critical/incidental findings and required specialist referral.
examTrap: Waiting for MRI in a time-sensitive condition when a faster validated emergency imaging pathway should happen first.
oneLinePearl: MRI is powerful because of tissue contrast, not because it is always the best first test.
sourceBasis: Canadian radiology safety and imaging practice

title: Nuclear Medicine: Functional Imaging Needs a Specific Physiologic Question
bottomLine: Nuclear medicine studies assess physiology, perfusion, metabolism or receptor uptake and should be ordered only when that functional information changes care. The tracer, pregnancy/lactation status, timing and alternative imaging matter; a nuclear study is not a generic replacement for CT/MRI/ultrasound.
recognize: Examples include V/Q scanning, myocardial perfusion, thyroid uptake, bone scans and PET-based oncologic imaging.
Different tracers and protocols answer different questions and have different preparation requirements.
differentiate: V/Q imaging can be useful when CT pulmonary angiography is unsuitable or local algorithms prefer it in selected patients.
PET uptake is not cancer-specific; infection/inflammation can also be metabolically active.
assessment: Clarify indication, pregnancy/lactation, renal function where relevant, prior imaging and medication/preparation requirements.
workup: Use specialty/radiology protocol to select the tracer and interpret the result alongside anatomic imaging and pretest probability.
management: Act on the diagnosis the study supports rather than treating uptake itself.
medicationSafety: Medication/iodine/thyroid preparation can alter some studies; verify protocol-specific requirements.
redFlags: Unstable patient needing faster definitive imaging
High-risk result requiring immediate specialty action
counselling: Explain the purpose of tracer-based functional imaging and any temporary radiation precautions.
followUp: Ensure result integration with the definitive diagnostic/treatment pathway.
examTrap: Ordering a nuclear study because it is 'more advanced' without identifying the physiologic question it answers.
oneLinePearl: Nuclear medicine maps function; order it when function changes the decision.

title: Screening Tests: Apply Them to the Right Asymptomatic Population
bottomLine: Screening is for asymptomatic people at defined risk. Interpret a screening result through prevalence, test characteristics and the downstream diagnostic pathway; symptoms or prior abnormalities move the patient out of routine screening into diagnostic evaluation.
recognize: Positive predictive value changes with disease prevalence and patient risk even when sensitivity/specificity are unchanged.
A positive screen is not a final diagnosis and a negative screen does not overrule concerning symptoms.
differentiate: Screening, surveillance and diagnosis are different clinical tasks.
Program eligibility/funding can differ from national evidence recommendations.
assessment: Confirm asymptomatic status, anatomy, age/risk, prior results, life expectancy/ability to benefit, family/genetic risk and access to follow-up.
workup: Use the current national/provincial screening pathway and its confirmatory testing sequence.
management: Offer evidence-based screening with shared decision-making where benefits/harms are preference sensitive and ensure abnormal results reach diagnostic resolution.
medicationSafety: Avoid pre-emptive treatment before the abnormal screen is confirmed unless a validated pathway specifically requires it.
redFlags: Symptoms being incorrectly routed to screening
High-risk family/genetic syndrome needing a different pathway
counselling: Explain false positives, false negatives and overdiagnosis in terms relevant to the actual test.
followUp: Track abnormal screening until definitive diagnostic closure.
examTrap: Using a routine screening test as the evaluation for a symptomatic patient.
oneLinePearl: Screen asymptomatic risk; diagnose symptoms.
sourceBasis: Canadian preventive health and provincial screening program principles

title: Sensitivity and Specificity: Pretest Probability Determines What a Result Means
bottomLine: Sensitivity and specificity describe test performance under defined conditions; they do not directly tell you the probability that this individual patient has disease. Combine pretest probability with likelihood ratios/results to estimate post-test probability and decide whether to rule out, confirm or test further.
recognize: High sensitivity can be useful for ruling out when the test is negative in an appropriate low/intermediate-risk setting; high specificity can support ruling in when positive.
Predictive values change with prevalence/pretest probability.
differentiate: A highly sensitive test is not automatically a good screening test if harms, false positives or feasibility are unacceptable.
A negative test cannot safely rule out disease when pretest probability is very high and the test is imperfect.
assessment: Estimate pretest probability before ordering the test and identify the treatment/testing threshold that matters clinically.
workup: Use validated clinical decision rules only in the populations/settings for which they were developed.
management: Choose testing only when the result can move probability across a meaningful decision threshold.
medicationSafety: Avoid exposing patients to treatment toxicity solely because a low-specificity test is positive without confirmatory evidence.
redFlags: High-risk disease being falsely dismissed after an insufficiently sensitive test
Low-risk patient harmed by cascades after indiscriminate testing
counselling: Explain uncertainty and why another test may or may not be useful after an initial result.
followUp: Reassess probability when new clinical information changes the pretest picture.
examTrap: Interpreting a positive result as the same disease probability in a low-risk screening population and a high-risk symptomatic population.
oneLinePearl: Test performance is fixed; what the result means changes with pretest probability.

title: Point-of-Care Testing: Fast Results Still Need Quality Control and Confirmation
bottomLine: Point-of-care testing is valuable when speed changes care, but analytic limits, specimen quality, operator competence and confirmatory requirements still apply. A surprising or high-consequence result should be reconciled with the clinical picture and laboratory confirmation when the device/pathway requires it.
recognize: POC glucose, pregnancy, urinalysis, respiratory pathogen, INR and selected chemistry tests can accelerate decisions.
Device performance and quality-control requirements vary substantially.
differentiate: A rapid screening result may be preliminary and may not have the same sensitivity/specificity as central laboratory testing.
Near-patient testing is not exempt from documentation, QC or infection-control requirements.
assessment: Confirm the test is validated for the patient/specimen/context and that the result will alter immediate management.
workup: Repeat or confirm discordant, implausible or high-consequence results according to the device and local laboratory policy.
management: Act immediately on validated emergency results while arranging confirmatory testing when necessary.
medicationSafety: Do not make irreversible medication decisions from an implausible POC result without checking device/specimen limitations.
redFlags: Critical result inconsistent with the patient
counselling: Explain when a rapid result is final versus preliminary and why confirmation may be required.
followUp: Document result, QC/confirmation pathway and responsibility for pending central-lab results.
examTrap: Assuming a fast result is automatically a more reliable result.
oneLinePearl: POC testing buys time—not immunity from quality standards.
sourceBasis: Canadian laboratory medicine and point-of-care quality principles

title: Microbiology Results: Infection, Colonization, Contamination, or Prior Exposure?
bottomLine: Microbiology results must be interpreted with specimen site/quality, symptoms, host risk and pretest probability. A positive test can represent infection, colonization, contamination or residual nucleic acid/antibody, while a negative test may reflect timing or sampling limitations.
recognize: Sterile-site growth generally has different significance from colonized-site cultures.
NAAT, culture, antigen and serology detect different biological signals and have different windows of positivity.
differentiate: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is not symptomatic UTI in most nonpregnant adults.
A positive respiratory/wound culture can represent colonization when the clinical syndrome does not support infection.
assessment: Define symptoms/source, immune status, prior antimicrobials, specimen quality/timing and whether the organism fits the syndrome.
workup: Repeat or obtain better specimens when contamination/poor quality is likely; use susceptibility testing and source-specific diagnostics when they change treatment.
management: Treat the patient/syndrome and source control, not the laboratory name alone; narrow/stop antimicrobials when evidence shows colonization or an alternate diagnosis.
medicationSafety: Unnecessary antimicrobial treatment causes resistance and adverse effects; drug selection should incorporate susceptibility, site penetration and organ function.
redFlags: Positive blood/CSF/other sterile-site result with compatible illness
counselling: Explain why a positive culture does not always require antibiotics and why some tests remain positive after infection resolves.
followUp: Review pending cultures/susceptibilities and public-health actions to completion.
examTrap: Treating a positive culture without first deciding whether the organism is causing the patient's syndrome.
oneLinePearl: Microbiology answers what was detected; clinical reasoning decides whether it is disease.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Medical Microbiology recommendations

title: Immunology Tests: Order the Antibody That Matches the Clinical Syndrome
bottomLine: Immunology testing has high false-positive potential when ordered without a compatible clinical syndrome. Start with phenotype and pretest probability, choose the specific validated antibody/complement/allergy test that answers the question, and interpret a positive result as supporting evidence rather than a stand-alone autoimmune or allergy diagnosis.
recognize: Autoantibodies can occur in healthy people and prevalence rises in some groups with age or other disease.
Allergy testing detects sensitization, which is not identical to clinical allergy; history of reproducible symptoms after exposure is essential.
differentiate: ANA may support a connective-tissue disease workup when symptoms fit but is a poor indiscriminate screen for nonspecific fatigue/pain.
Food-specific IgG reflects exposure and is not a validated diagnostic test for food allergy/intolerance.
assessment: Define the syndrome first: inflammatory joints, rash/photosensitivity, Raynaud, sicca, vasculitis signs, recurrent infections, immediate allergic reactions or other organ-specific features.
For allergy, document exact exposure, timing, reproducibility, cofactors and severity before choosing skin/specific-IgE testing.
workup: Order targeted autoantibodies/complement/immunoglobulins/specific IgE only when the result can change diagnosis or management; avoid broad panels with no hypothesis.
Confirm unusual or high-consequence results through specialty/laboratory pathways when assay limitations or cross-reactivity matter.
management: Treat the clinical disease, not antibody positivity. Refer patients with significant systemic autoimmune disease, immune deficiency or complex allergy/anaphylaxis to the appropriate specialty pathway.
medicationSafety: Do not start immunosuppression solely for a positive autoantibody without compatible disease activity.
Do not prescribe broad elimination diets or epinephrine solely from unvalidated food-IgG testing.
redFlags: Severe recurrent/opportunistic infection suggesting immune deficiency
counselling: Explain that a positive antibody can mean susceptibility or sensitization rather than definite disease and that testing must match symptoms.
followUp: Close the loop on specialty referral and avoid repeating stable autoantibodies when the result no longer changes management.
examTrap: Ordering a broad autoimmune panel for nonspecific fatigue and diagnosing disease from the first weakly positive antibody.
oneLinePearl: Immunology testing is phenotype first, antibody second.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Allergy & Clinical Immunology recommendations

title: Genetic Testing: Consent, the Right Test, and a Plan for Every Possible Result
bottomLine: Genetic testing should answer a defined diagnostic, predictive, reproductive or treatment question. Before ordering, establish informed consent, choose the narrowest appropriate test strategy, discuss possible positive/negative/uncertain/incidental results and family implications, and ensure genetic counselling/specialty follow-up is available for results that can materially affect care.
recognize: Testing may clarify a clinical diagnosis, inherited cancer/cardiac risk, reproductive risk, pharmacogenomic question or eligibility for targeted therapy.

A negative result can be uninformative when the familial variant is unknown or the test does not cover the suspected mechanism; a variant of uncertain significance is not a confirmed pathogenic diagnosis.
differentiate: Diagnostic, carrier, predictive/presymptomatic, prenatal and newborn screening tests have different consent and interpretation issues.
Direct-to-consumer results may require clinical confirmation before they guide medical decisions.
assessment: Build a three-generation family history when relevant, document age of onset/ancestry/consanguinity and define how the result would change surveillance, treatment or reproductive planning.
Assess the patient's goals, understanding, privacy concerns and readiness for information that may affect relatives.
workup: Use syndrome-specific criteria and genetics/laboratory guidance to select targeted variant, gene panel, chromosomal or broader genomic testing rather than defaulting to the largest panel.
Refer to genetic counselling/clinical genetics when results are complex, predictive, reproductive, familial or likely to create significant psychosocial/management implications.
management: Act only on pathogenic/likely pathogenic results and other validated findings within the relevant guideline; do not manage a variant of uncertain significance as confirmed disease.
Cascade testing/surveillance for relatives should follow genetics guidance and consent/privacy requirements.
medicationSafety: Pharmacogenomic results are drug/gene/context specific and do not replace medication history, organ function and interaction review.
Do not alter high-stakes treatment from an unconfirmed direct-to-consumer genetic result.
redFlags: Result indicating a highly penetrant actionable cancer/cardiac syndrome
Newborn/child with suspected metabolic genetic emergency
Pregnancy with time-sensitive fetal genetic concern
Unexpected result with major family implications and no counselling plan
counselling: Discuss benefits, limits, uncertain/incidental findings, possible implications for biological relatives and the patient's right to informed decision-making.
Avoid promising complete certainty; genetics often changes probability and surveillance rather than providing a binary answer.
followUp: Ensure results are interpreted by the appropriate clinician/genetics service and that surveillance/treatment/cascade-testing plans are documented and closed-loop.
examTrap: Treating a variant of uncertain significance as proof of an inherited disease—or ordering broad genetic testing without discussing possible outcomes and family implications.
oneLinePearl: A genetic test is not finished when the lab reports—it is finished when the result is interpreted, counselled and acted on appropriately.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Genetic Counsellors resources
